## Function assignment and case

*She was handing him some broccoli.*

| Selected pronoun | Assigned function | Form |
|---|---|---|
| Feminine | Nominative / subject | **she** |
| Masculine | Dative / recipient object | **him** |

If the functions are exchanged: *He was handing her some broccoli.*

::: {.prompt}
Why do we get *he* and *her*, rather than *him* and *she*?
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, I and III.A
:::

## Assigning nominative first

> "... at least in English, there is a preference for combinations of elements
> that permit the nominative function to be assigned first."

*She seems to be feeding the dog.*

::: {.prompt}
What must the speaker have planned before assigning nominative to *she*?
Which verb determines her role in the event: *seems* or *feeding*?
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, III.B.2, p. 966; classroom example
:::

## Function words and affixes

For a definite, plural noun phrase: *the goats*.

| | Garrett | Lapointe and Dell |
|---|---|---|
| Article *the* | Already in the frame | Inserted into a definite determiner slot |
| Plural *-s* | Already in the frame | Already in the frame |
| Stem *goat* | Supplied separately | Supplied separately |

In Lapointe's aphasia data, function words tended to be **omitted**;
affixes tended to be **replaced**.

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, V.A and V.B; example adapted from their definite plural NP
:::

## Inflectional stranding

Intended: *You **ended** up **ordering** some fish dish.*

Produced: *You **ordered** up **ending** some fish dish.*

| | First verb | Second verb |
|---|---|---|
| Intended | **end** + ed | **order** + ing |
| Produced | **order** + ed | **end** + ing |

The stems exchange; the inflections stay. Both frame accounts predict this.

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, V.C; Garrett, cited as in press
:::

## Plural number and its realization

| Selected noun | SINGULAR | PLURAL |
|---|---|---|
| *goat* | goat | goat + **s** |
| *sheep* | sheep | sheep |

**PLURAL** is a grammatical feature. Its realization depends on the noun.

::: {.prompt}
*Two sheep are outside.* Which word shows number agreement, even though
*sheep* has no plural suffix?
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, V.C; classroom sentence
:::

## How does the verb get its number?

*The **key** to the cabinets **is** missing.*

*The **keys** to the cabinet **are** missing.*

| In the first sentence | What gets specified |
|---|---|
| Subject head | *key*: SINGULAR |
| Agreement | The finite verb receives the subject's number |
| Realization | Present-tense *be*, third-person singular: **is** |

Attraction error: *The key to the cabinets **are** missing.*

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, V.C; classroom examples
:::

## Which property causes attraction?

*The picture of the ___ **is** on the wall.*

| Local noun | Grammatical number | Ends in /s/ or /z/? |
|---|---|---|
| cabinet | Singular | No |
| cabinets | Plural | Yes |
| children | Plural | No |
| rose | Singular | Yes |

In the studies reviewed, **grammatical plurality** reliably caused attraction,
including when the plural was irregular.

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, V.C; Bock & Miller 1991; Bock & Eberhard 1993; classroom items
:::

## Agreement across a clause boundary

**Phrase:** *The claim [about the newborn babies] ...*

**Clause:** *The claim [that wolves had raised the babies] ...*

In both, singular *claim* requires **was**. Plural *babies* can attract **were**.

::: {.fragment}
Errors were more likely after phrase modifiers. Putting *babies* in an
embedded clause reduced its interference with main-clause agreement.
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, III.C; Bock & Cutting 1992
:::

## Design an agreement experiment {.smaller}

| Modifier | Singular local noun | Plural local noun |
|---|---|---|
| Phrase | The claim about the newborn baby ... | The claim about the newborn babies ... |
| Clause | The claim that wolves had raised the baby ... | The claim that wolves had raised the babies ... |

Groups of three, ten minutes:

1. Write one new item in all four versions.
2. Specify how you will elicit and score agreement.
3. Predict where speakers will produce a plural verb in error.
4. Identify one confound and address it.

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, III.C; class exercise based on Bock & Cutting 1992
:::

## Change the subject

*She **was** hand**ing** him some broccoli.*

| Grammatical information | Realization in this sentence |
|---|---|
| Subject and object functions | **she**, **him** |
| Past progressive | **was** + hand**ing** |
| Singular subject agreement | **was** |

::: {.prompt}
Replace *she* with *they*. Which forms change? Which stay?
Where does the information for each change come from?
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, VI, Fig. 6; classroom comparison
:::
